name: Cardinality-Constrained / Fixed-Cardinality Subset Sum (the Hamming layer of Subset Sum; k-item subset sum; (C,k)-SUM)
description: Cardinality-constrained subset sum asks, given n integers a_1,...,a_n, a target t, and a cardinality k (or a vector of k targets for k-Subset Sum), whether some subset S of exactly k items satisfies sum_{i in S} a_i = t. Equivalently, the search is restricted to the Hamming layer of weight k inside {0,1}^n. It is a distinct structural variant because the cardinality (support size / Hamming weight) is an additive resource that can be tracked alongside the sum: the pair (sum, |S|) is additive under disjoint union, so both dynamic programming and meet-in-the-middle extend to it cheaply. It appears in the literature in several guises: (i) k-Subset Sum with k disjoint subsets and k targets (Antonopoulos-Pagourtzis-Petsalakis-Vasilakis); (ii) (C,k)-SUM, the subset-balancing problem with coefficient set C whose solutions have exactly k nonzero coefficients (Randolph-Wegrzycki); (iii) low/fixed Hamming-weight subset sum, as used in low-weight discrete-logarithm and decoding cryptanalysis (Esser-May); and (iv) the Pigeonhole/Either-Or regime where a solution of cardinality about n/2 is guaranteed. In the representation/mixing technique for worst-case subset balancing, the algorithm guesses the solution's cardinality/support profile, and the 'mixing' step is precisely about spreading candidate vectors across Hamming layers and residue classes; cardinality control (via random restrictions) is therefore intrinsic to the mixing argument rather than an afterthought.
worst_case_time: There is no single canonical bound; the answer depends on whether k is a constant, part of the input, or about n/2. (a) For constant k in the k-SUM parameterization, meet-in-the-middle gives O_k(n^{ceil(k/2)}) time (the classical k-SUM bound; recorded for (C,k)-SUM as MITM running in O_k(n^{ceil(k/2)}) in Randolph's thesis). (b) For general k given as input, the standard exact pseudo-polynomial algorithm is a Bellman-style DP with an extra cardinality dimension, O(n k t) time (equivalently O(n t) per fixed cardinality), where t = target; exhaustive enumeration costs O(C(n,k)) = O(n^k) for small k. (c) Cardinality-constrained k-Subset Sum (k disjoint target subsets, with cardinality constraints on the solution subsets) can be solved in deterministic O~(n^{k/(k+1)} t^k) and randomized O~(n + t^k) time by FFT/color-coding methods building on Koiliaris-Xu and Bringmann (Antonopoulos et al., JOCO 2023/arXiv 2112.04244). (d) For the low-Hamming-weight cryptanalytic regime, the best known subset-sum algorithm is heuristic and runs in 2^{0.645n} with polynomial memory (Esser-May, EUROCRYPT 2020), improving BCJ's 2^{0.72n} random-subset-sum bound; it requires many solutions and is not a worst-case exact bound. (e) For k = Theta(n) in the worst case the problem inherits the general Subset Sum barrier: no O*(2^{(1/2-eps)n}) algorithm is known.
space_complexity: Cardinality-augmented DP: O(k t) (or O(t) with a decision-only formulation plus implicit cardinality tracking; the natural table storing both sum and count is O(k t) = O(n t)). Explicit O(t) space with recursive divide-and-conquer is achievable for the boolean version. Meet-in-the-middle: O(n^{ceil(k/2)}) pair storage for constant k, or O(2^{n/2}) for the vanilla split with cardinality pairs. The Esser-May low-weight algorithms use polynomial memory O(n^{Theta(1)}), which is their main selling point over memory-heavy representation methods.
model: Unit-cost RAM / word RAM for DP and meet-in-the-middle (the cardinality coordinate is an O(log n)-bit integer, so it fits word operations cheaply). The FFT/color-coding k-Subset Sum algorithms (Koiliaris-Xu, Bringmann, Antonopoulos et al.) are stated on the word RAM / algebraic (FFT) model. Esser-May is stated in the generic group/collision-finding model with polynomial memory.
randomized_or_deterministic: Mixed. DP and the plain cardinality-filtered meet-in-the-middle are deterministic. The k-Subset Sum algorithms of Antonopoulos et al. come in both a deterministic O~(n^{k/(k+1)} t^k) variant and a randomized O~(n + t^k) variant. Esser-May's low-weight subset-sum algorithms are randomized heuristics (collision finding).
time_space_tradeoff_curve: Mostly single point, but the cardinality-filtered meet-in-the-middle inherits the classical Schroeppel-Shamir tradeoff: enumerating pairs by (sum, cardinality) still costs about the size of the largest Hamming layer, so space can be traded against the number of lists scanned. A precise time-space tradeoff curve specialized to fixed cardinality is not stated in the sources reviewed [uncertain].
numerical_exponent_and_record_year: Constant-k k-SUM/(C,k)-SUM meet-in-the-middle exponent ceil(k/2) in the number of items (classical, Horowitz-Sahni 1974 for k=2; recorded for (C,k)-SUM in Randolph's 2024 thesis). Low-Hamming-weight subset sum base-2 exponent 0.645 (Esser-May, EUROCRYPT 2020, record year 2020), improving 0.72 (Becker-Coron-Joux 2011). k-Sum with constant doubling constant C: O~(C^{ceil(k/2)} 2^{O(k)} n), matching the k-SUM-conjecture lower bound up to a C factor (Randolph-Wegrzycki, ESA 2024). Cardinality-constrained k-Subset Sum is pseudo-polynomial, so its 'exponent' is in t, not in n (Antonopoulos et al., 2023).
problem_variant: Cardinality-constrained / fixed-cardinality Subset Sum (exactly k items), k-Subset Sum (k disjoint subsets with k targets), (C,k)-SUM (exactly k nonzero coefficients over coefficient set C), low/fixed Hamming-weight Subset Sum, and the balanced-solution slice (k ~ n/2) of vanilla Subset Sum, Partition and Equal-Subset-Sum.
applies_to: Exact decision and search when the cardinality of the chosen subset is fixed to k (or is one of a small set of allowed cardinalities), including the search restricted to a single Hamming layer of {0,1}^n and the multiple-target k-Subset Sum. Also applies to subset balancing with bounded coefficient set C when the number of nonzero coefficients is fixed. Restriction: fixing the cardinality does not by itself remove worst-case hardness.
coefficient_set: C = {0,1} for vanilla fixed-cardinality Subset Sum (each item chosen at most once, exactly k chosen). C = {-1,0,1} for fixed-support Equal-Subset-Sum / Partition formulations. General constant-size C (e.g. C = [-d:d] or C = [±d]) for (C,k)-SUM, where the cardinality is the number of nonzero coefficients; |C| affects the k-SUM base (C^{ceil(k/2)}).
density_regime: Density-agnostic in the worst-case parameterization; the cardinality constraint is a Hamming-weight restriction, not a density restriction. The low-Hamming-weight cryptanalytic algorithms (Esser-May) target dense random instances with a_i in Z_{2^n} (many representations), which is the opposite of the low-density lattice-solvable regime.
solution_regime: General decision/search for arbitrary k. A special promised regime is the pigeonhole/balanced case k ~ n/2, where a solution is frequently guaranteed and where representation/mixing methods count overlapping Hamming balls; this is the regime relevant to Equal-Subset-Sum and Pigeonhole Equal Subset Sum. Randolph's 'Either-Or' subset sum is a related 1-bit random-restriction variant.
cardinality_constraint: Yes - the fixed-cardinality/Hamming-layer constraint is the defining feature of this item. Cardinality is treated as an explicit additive coordinate in DP and meet-in-the-middle, and as the solution profile/support size that is guessed and controlled in the representation-mixing technique and in bounded-coefficient balancing.
key_technique: Track cardinality as a second additive dimension: (i) Bellman/DP with a count coordinate, O(n k t); (ii) meet-in-the-middle matching pairs with equal (sum, cardinality), giving the k-SUM O_k(n^{ceil(k/2)}) bound; (iii) color coding for disjoint target subsets (CardColorCodingLayer, Antonopoulos et al.) and FFT-based modified characteristic polynomials with one extra variable per cardinality; (iv) in subset balancing, guess the solution's support/profile and use random restrictions to force the candidate solution into a chosen Hamming layer, with a mixing dichotomy ensuring that failure-to-mix implies an unbalanced or numerous-solution instance solvable elsewhere; (v) nested collision finding with polynomial memory for the low-weight regime (Esser-May).
core_idea: Cardinality is additive and cheap: |S| obeys |S ∪ T| = |S| + |T| for disjoint S, T, so the pair (subset sum, subset size) behaves like a two-coordinate knapsack and can be stored/enumerated as easily as the sum alone. Meet-in-the-middle over (sum, cardinality) reduces fixed-cardinality Subset Sum to a member of the k-SUM family, where the birthday tradeoff gives the n^{ceil(k/2)} exponent. In the balanced case k ~ n/2 the largest Hamming layer has size about 2^n/sqrt(n), which is within a polynomial factor of 2^n and of the MITM space, so the cardinality restriction alone provides essentially no worst-case savings; the useful structure comes from controlling which layer the solution lies in and how many representations it has.
reduction_pipeline: Fixed-cardinality Subset Sum -> k-SUM / (C,k)-SUM by appending the cardinality as a coordinate (and, for disjoint targets, by dimensional lifting to k sum-coordinates plus cardinality coordinates). In the representation/mixing direction the pipeline is reversed: a bounded-coefficient Subset Balancing instance is analyzed layer by layer over candidate Hamming weights, random restrictions pin the candidate weight, and modular filtering (representation technique) selects vectors that can recombine into a weight-k solution. Low-weight Subset Sum is also the search problem underlying low-weight discrete-logarithm cryptanalysis.
constructive_vs_existential: Constructive: all the algorithmic variants (DP, MITM, color coding, collision finding) can return the actual k-subset when one exists; the pigeonhole/existential arguments for guaranteed solutions are converted into witnesses by the corresponding constructive algorithms.
search_vs_decision_witness: Both: decides whether a k-item subset sums to t and, because the methods are constructive, returns an explicit witness (the k-subset, or the k disjoint subsets for k-Subset Sum). Constructivity is direct and unconditional for the deterministic algorithms.
obstacle_to_2n3: Fixing the cardinality does not by itself lower the exponent of vanilla worst-case Subset Sum: the hard balanced case k ~ n/2 lives in the largest Hamming layer, and the fixed-cardinality problem there is essentially the original problem with a polynomial-factor change in list size. The k-SUM conjecture asserts that the O_k(n^{ceil(k/2)}) meet-in-the-middle bound is optimal for k-SUM up to polynomial factors, so the cardinality parameterization is expected to be a barrier, not a route, toward 2^{n/3}. Any attempt to exploit cardinality to reach O*(2^{n/3}) must additionally leverage structure (small doubling constant, bounded coefficient set, or many representations), which is exactly where the worst-case representation-mixing line operates and where the C = [±1] Partition case currently resists.
potential_to_break_mitm: Low for the general fixed-cardinality problem in isolation. Medium as an analytical lens and as a component: cardinality control is central to the mixing step of the worst-case representation technique and to bounded-coefficient balancing, and (C,k)-SUM is provably easier when the doubling constant is small (Randolph-Wegrzycki). On sparse, unstructured, balanced-cardinality instances the MITM barrier is expected to remain.
barrier_evidence: The k-SUM conjecture (for every k >= 3 there is no O(n^{ceil(k/2)-eps}) algorithm) and the 3SUM conjecture constrain the constant-k case; SETH and the Strong k-SUM Hypothesis give matching conditional lower bounds for the pseudopolynomial/dense regime. Cardinality-constrained optimization parameterized by k alone is W[1]-hard / W-hard in general (naive enumeration is XP, O(n^k)), so no fixed-parameter tractable algorithm in k alone is expected for arbitrary binary-encoded weights. No unconditional lower bound rules out a 2^{(1/2-eps)n} worst-case algorithm for fixed-cardinality Subset Sum.
open_questions: Is there a worst-case O*(2^{(1/2-eps)n}) algorithm for fixed-cardinality Subset Sum with k ~ n/2? Can the cardinality-controlled mixing dichotomy and random-restriction machinery be pushed from bounded-coefficient balancing to C = [±1] (Partition) and fixed-cardinality {0,1} Subset Sum? Are there matching lower bounds for fixed-cardinality Subset Sum beyond the k-SUM conjecture? Can polynomial-memory low-weight techniques (Esser-May) be derandomized or given worst-case guarantees? Does parameterizing by both k and the doubling constant yield optimally efficient algorithms (the current (C,k)-SUM bound has a C-factor gap)? How do bounded-coefficient balancing algorithms behave when the solution's Hamming layer is sparse?
conditional_hypothesis: The k-SUM conjecture (no O(n^{ceil(k/2)-eps}) for constant k), the 3SUM conjecture, SETH and the Strong k-SUM Hypothesis (pseudopolynomial/dense lower bounds), and the unproven Meet-in-the-Middle / Subset Sum hypothesis for the 2^{n/2} exponent. No hardness assumption is needed for the positive algorithms.
worst_case_vs_average_case_guarantee: DP, meet-in-the-middle and the deterministic k-Subset Sum algorithms give worst-case guarantees. The Esser-May 2^{0.645n} low-weight result is a heuristic/average-case bound for random subset-sum instances with many representations, not a worst-case guarantee. The (C,k)-SUM constant-doubling algorithm is worst-case within its structural restriction (bounded doubling constant).
cryptographic_regime: Relevant. Low-Hamming-weight subset sum and low-weight discrete logarithm are the cryptanalytic face of the cardinality-constrained problem; Esser-May (EUROCRYPT 2020) use low-weight subset-sum/dlog algorithms in the dense random regime (a_i in Z_{2^n}) to attack cryptographic parameters, and representation/collision methods with cardinality control are standard in knapsack and decoding (syndrome decoding finds low-weight vectors). The relevant regime is dense/random with many solutions, contrasting with the low-density lattice-solvable regime.
pseudopolynomial_interaction: Strong and intrinsic. The most direct exact algorithm is the cardinality-augmented pseudo-polynomial DP, O(n k t); the k-Subset Sum FFT/color-coding algorithms of Antonopoulos et al. are pseudo-polynomial O~(n^{k/(k+1)} t^k) and O~(n + t^k); and the whole pseudopolynomial theory of Subset Sum (Bellman, Koiliaris-Xu, Bringmann) extends to the cardinality-constrained version by carrying a count coordinate. This is complementary to the exponential meet-in-the-middle regime.

empirical_evidence: Mostly theoretical. Empirical data on fixed-cardinality instances is limited: Pisinger's core/knapsack experiments show that cardinality constraints help branch-and-bound via Lagrangian bounds, and cryptanalytic papers (Esser-May and successors) report estimated exponents rather than large benchmark tables for the fixed-weight subset-sum problem. No systematic public benchmark of fixed-cardinality subset-sum solvers was found [uncertain].
implementation_artifact: No canonical repository dedicated to the cardinality-constrained variant. Standard cardinality-aware DP and meet-in-the-middle implementations are widely available (e.g. competitive-programming references and the Pisinger knapsack codes at https://hjemmesider.diku.dk/~pisinger/codes.html, which include cardinality-constraint bounds); Esser-May-style low-weight collision algorithms are implemented in the lattice/ISD tooling ecosystem but no single official artifact was confirmed [uncertain].
verification_method: Reproduce the cardinality-augmented Bellman DP (state (i, count, sum)) and compare against brute-force enumeration of all C(n,k) k-subsets on small random instances. For meet-in-the-middle, verify the O_k(n^{ceil(k/2)}) behavior by enumerating (sum, cardinality) pairs in halves and matching complementary pairs. For the k-Subset Sum algorithms, check the FFT/color-coding construction and the extra cardinality variables against the Antonopoulos et al. paper. For the low-weight/Esser-May claims, reproduce the collision-finding recursion and confirm the 2^{0.645n} exponent under the stated random-instance model.
